## Mapping photovoltaic power stations and assessing their environmental impacts from multi-sensor datasets in Massachusetts, United States

## Shiqi Tao[a] , John Rogan[a] , Su Ye[b][,][ *] , Nicholas Geron[a]

a _Graduate School of Geography, Clark University, Worcester, MA, 01610, USA_

b _Department of Natural Resources and the Environment, University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, 06269, USA_

|A R T I C L E I N F O_Keywords:_DeforestationEnvironmental changeImage segmentationTime series analysisPhotovoltaic power stationsSolar panels|A B S T R A C T|
|---|---|
||Solar energy is often viewed as a sustainable alternative to non-renewable energy, yet the debatebetween solar energy promotion and environmental cost has received growing attention. Accu-rate geographic information of photovoltaic power stations is a prerequisite for quantifying costand benefit of clean energy promotion. Therefore, this study aims to estimate the environmentalimpacts of photovoltaic power stations by geo-mapping solar panels over space and time. Basedon the case of Massachusetts, United States, we classified the solar panel arrays using object-based image analysis on Sentinel-2 monthly composites, identified the per-array constructionyear based upon 20-year all available Landsat time-series dataset, and assessed the solar-inducedenvironmental impacts with various environmental datasets. The accuracy assessment suggeststhat our classification performs well for detecting solar arrays (overall accuracy: 96%), depictingphotovoltaic power stations geometry (average Jaccard Index value: 0.70), and capturing theconstruction years (percentage of temporal bias less than one year: 73%). Solar-induced land useand cover changes have largely occurred in forest and cropland, where 49% and 23% of the solararrays have been installed, respectively. Geographic Information System (GIS) analysis uncoversthat more than half of the mapped solar arrays were built in proximity (within 500 m) to rarewildlife habitats or adjacent to wetlands. This work exemplifies a new framework for identifyingmultifaceted land change information through a combination of finer-resolution Sentinel-2 im-ages and long Landsat-based data archive. The findings can be useful for informing spatial plan-ning and contributing to the growth, expansion, advancement, and location selection of solar in-stallation arrays. The study also provides a new perspective for monitoring forest loss due toclean energy promotion and addressing critical issues of local conflicts between solar energy andenvironmental conservation.|

## **1. Introduction**

Aiming at achieving sustainable development, many countries are promoting the transition from traditional energy sources to alternatives that are new and cleaner (Shahsavari and Akbari, 2018). Among these alternatives, solar energy has been viewed as the most promising source for sustainable energy consumption due mostly to its naturally high availability and relatively low negative impacts on the environment (Panwar et al., 2011; Solangi et al., 2011; Bahadori and Nwaoha, 2013). A recent study suggests that the

use of solar energy as a substitute for the commonly used fossil fuels is estimated to reduce 69–100 million tons of carbon dioxide ( _CO_ 2) by 2030 (Shahsavari and Akbari, 2018).

Despite its potential of combating energy crises arising from exhaustible sources, solar energy development may still bear the risks of inducing non-trivial environmental impacts. One critical aspect pertains to the location selection for solar panels. Solar-induced impacts can be multitudinal, involving dramatic land conversions or modifications that could yield substantial and long-lasting impacts on the surrounding environments. To date, while some solar panel datasets are publicly available (Bradbury et al., 2016; Kruitwagen et al., 2021), they are provided with only location information without detailed per-facility attributes such as geometry, size and construction history. With the accelerating pace of seeking solar energy and developing solar sites by many countries (Prăvălie et al., 2019), it is more imperative than ever to accurately map the solar energy infrastructure at a high spatial resolution and quantify their land cover change impacts.

Remote sensing has been recognized as an effective way for the target-based mapping (Zhang et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2018), with a potential of characterizing its history from its long data records (Ye et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2022). Compared to other urban objects, solar fields are a relatively small-sized (1000–50,000 m[2] ), characterized by high within-object spectral variability, due to the varying material types, installation angles, and background covers (Edun et al., 2021), suggesting that a fine-resolution (<=10 m) mapping is necessitated. The Sentinel-2 satellites, launched by the European Space Agency (ESA) (Drusch et al., 2012), provides a cost-effective means for mapping such-like urban targets with a 10-m resolution and 13 spectral bands ranging from the visual range to the shortwave infrared (SWIR). Yet, the approach for accurately identifying solar panels from heterogeneous urban environment and natural landscape is still under investigation. Moreover, the relatively shorter history of Sentinel-2 dataset limits the retrospective analysis, implicating the need of incorporating a long-history archive such as Landsat-based datasets which could provide 40-year near-continuous observations. The integration of Sentinel-2 and Landsat time series will offer a complementary and multifaceted view for solar panel development, enabling a more thorough examination for their both spatial and temporal properties (Zhu et al., 2022).

Using the case of Massachusetts in the United States, this study aims to fill this gap by geo-mapping the installations of solar photovoltaic panel sites and quantifying their potential effects on the natural environment. This research could be conceptualized into three different objectives. The first objective is the geo-mapping of photovoltaic power stations including their locations, shapes, and extents with Sentinel-2 high spatial resolution images in 2020. The second objective is the identification of the construction year of each mapped solar site and the associated pre-installation land cover using historical Landsat time-series datasets. The third objective is the evaluation of environmental impacts of the installed solar sites with geospatial analysis on important ecosystems and natural landscapes.

## **2. Study area**

Our study area is the whole Massachusetts (MA), USA (Fig. 1). Our training and validation sets (133 demarcated solar fields) were mainly selected from three MA counties (a total area of 4931 km[2] ), including Franklin, Hampshire, and Hampden, because we have a relatively complete dataset including the footprints of all large photovoltaic power stations provided by Harvard Forest.

Three main types of installed solar panels were found in MA (Fig. 2). The first type is characterized by ground-mounted large-size solar panel array fields situated in vacant land (Fig. 2a), most of which are surrounded by forest cover. These fields are occupied by photovoltaic power stations in large patches, also known as solar farms or solar parks. The second type (Fig. 2b) is the rooftopinstalled panels on large buildings or otherwise over parking lots. The third type (Fig. 2c) is typically installed on the rooftop of private houses in relatively small sizes which generates energy mainly for private use in households. In this study, we will focus on mapping the first type of solar installation, namely photovoltaic power stations, because they have the greatest direct impacts on the ecosystem. A solar field of the first type often consists of two elements. One element includes solar arrays identified as solar panels

## **3. Data and methods**

For our first objective, we used the Sentinel-2A dataset, object-based image segmentation and random forest classifier to identify – solar arrays. For the second objective, we obtained all available historical Landsat images during 1983 2020 and applied the COLD algorithm to extract construction years of each detected solar array. With a regard to the third objective, we assessed the environmental impacts by overlaying the photovoltaic power station data with forest cover, wetland, and protected areas. The flowchart of the whole process is shown in Fig. 3.

## _3.1. Data_

## _3.1.1. Sentinel-2 and Landsat data_

The study area consists of nine Sentinel-2 scenes (T18TXM, T18TXN, T18TYN, T19TBG, T19TCG, T19TCH, T19TDG, T19TCF, T19TDF). To minimize influence of atmospheric conditions, Sentinel-2 Level-2A data were used to provide the Bottom of Atmosphere reflectance images. We selected only visible and near-infrared bands because they have a relatively finer spatial resolution (10 m). For each image, clouds were screened out by the cloud mask band (i.e., the QA60 band). Then, we performed pixel-based medium compositing to generate seven cloud-free monthly images from April to October 2020.

All Landsat ARD Tier 1 surface reflectance products between 1983 and 2020 (38 years) for five tiles (Tile IDs ‘30/06’, ‘30/05’, ‘31/06’, ‘29/06’, and ‘29/05’) were downloaded from the USGS Earth Resources Observation and Science (EROS) center. The Landsat ARD products gridded all available Landsat-4, and -5 TM, Landsat-7 ETM+ and Landsat-8 OLI/TIRS (Thermal Infrared Sensor), and were provided as tiled, geo-registered, and atmospherically corrected products, which were defined in a common equal area projection (Dwyer et al., 2018).

## _3.1.2. Ancillary data_

Ancillary data used for the solar panel mapping include 1) the cropland data layer (CDL) provided by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), 2) the photovoltaic power station footprint information provided by Harvard Forest, 3) solar plant location dataset from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and 4) the ecosystem function layers. USDA CDL is a 30-m national crop-specific land cover data but also contain information on other land cover types; the Harvard Forest solar footprints is a GIS dataset consisting of all large-area solar sites in the three pilot counties, which were manually delineated through extensive visual interpretation based on high-resolution images in Google Earth; the EIA location data of solar plants is a comprehensive solar plant dataset with geolocation information generated by survey forms; the ecosystem function datasets include three specific layers for wetland,[1] pond/lake & riverine,[2] and rare wildlife habitats,[3] which will be mainly used to assess impacts of photovoltaic power stations on ecosystem services.

## _3.2. Mapping solar panel installations with Sentinel-2 images_

## _3.2.1. Creating solar array segments_

Considering solar panel installations may cause heterogeneous spectral reflectance in a remotely sensed image due to their varying angles of deployment (Edun et al., 2021), we performed an image segmentation to generate image objects for object-based classification. The composited Sentinel-2 images were segmented using the Simple Non-Iterative Clustering (SNIC) algorithm (Achanta and Susstrunk, 2017). SNIC forms pixel clusters by measuring spectral similarity and enforcing the connectivity of neighborhood image pixels. Compared to other segmentation algorithms such as Simple Linear Iterative Clustering, SNIC is memory-saving with relatively fewer parameters.

## _3.2.2. Mapping solar array_

We adopted a two-step classification method to identify the image pixels occupied by solar panels. The first step is to generate a solar panel potential layer from the CDL data layer to exclude the regions that were obviously not solar panels. We calculated the frequency of each USDA CDL land cover class within our sampled solar fields and found that solar panels mainly fall within two major classes, i.e., grassland and urban land. Therefore, the classes of urban land and bare land were defined as _Class Ap_ , while others are the background category _Class Bn_ . We adopted a stratified sampling design to randomly select pixels of Class _Ap_ and Class _Bn_ . Considering high uncertainties of training samples exist at the boundary of the two classes, we used a 3 by 3 spatial filtering method to filter out the sample pixels (both _Ap_ and _Bn_ ) which have different categories with any of the neighboring pixels (Fig. 4). As pixels of solar farms have relatively low NDVI values, we empirically set a value of 0.3 as the threshold to exclude the _Ap_ samples whose NDVI values are above the threshold. As a result, a sample size of 800 and 1000 were remained for Class _Ap_ and Class _Bn_ , respectively. Using the refined sample set, we applied the random forest (Breiman, 2001) machine learning algorithm (tree number = 500) to classify the segmented Sentinel-2 image so that the potential layer for solar panels (Class _Ap_ ) could be derived.

The second step is to accurately delineate solar panel boundaries from the potential layer. We selected a total of 10,000 initial sample pixels using a stratified sampling: within Class _Ap_ , we visually demarcated 1047 solar panels (excluding the gap between adjacent solar panels) consisting of over 5000 pixels, which are distributed across the three pilot study counties. Meanwhile, we randomly selected 5000 pixels outside the footprint of solar panels to represent areas without the occupation of the solar panels. We reserved 500 pixels of each type (solar panel vs. otherwise) for the testing purpose. We designed several sampling schemes to test effects of different training sample sizes and different proportions of the solar panel sample. Specifically, the training sample size increased from 1000 to 5000 with an increment of 1,000, while the proportion of solar panel pixels in the sample increased from 0.2 to 0.8 with an increment of 0.2, leading to a total of 20 schemes in combination. We selected the sampling scheme with the highest accuracy level based on the independent testing samples, i.e., a total sample of 5000 pixels with 40% of solar pixels. Using this combination of solar fields and other land cover samples, we trained a random forest algorithm.

Lastly, we overlaid the binary classification map and segmentation maps from the first step and identified the solar panel arrays as the segments that have >50% pixels classified as ‘photovoltaic power stations’.

## _3.2.3. Post-classification editing for the demarcation of solar array boundaries_

We removed the solar-panel polygons with an area less than 500 _m_[2] and performed a dilation of 2 pixels followed by an erosion of 2 pixels. Each of the remaining solar polygons was then visually checked using the composited Sentinel image of October 2020, backed up by referencing high-resolution data from Google Earth. We deleted the solar fields which were obviously misclassified and refined the polygon boundaries of the remaining polygons if the overlap with the visually interpreted solar fields was less than 90% of the interpreted fields.

## _3.3. Identification of solar construction year and detection of surrounding cleared land_

We applied the COLD (Zhu et al., 2020) algorithm to identify the installation years for all solar arrays in MA using Landsat-based time series. COLD was designed to detect all types of land disturbance using all available Landsat images and has shown its capability for mapping complex urban change (Liu et al., 2019; Aljaddani et al., 2022). COLD first applies the FMASK and TMASK algorithms (Zhu and Woodcock, 2014a) to mask out the cloud, cloud shadows, and snow in each image (Zhu et al., 2015a), and then builds a har-

## _3.4. Map accuracy assessment_

The accuracy of solar panel detection will be reported mainly from the two aspects. First, the object-level thematic and geometric quality were evaluated using a confusion matrix and Jaccard Index based on our validation datasets from three pilot countries; second, the bias of the identified construction year was estimated based on the EIA data.

## _3.4.1. Validation for the classified photovoltaic power stations_

We quantified the classification errors based on both pixel (point-based) evaluation and segment evaluation (Ye et al., 2018) using the sample located within the three pilot counties of Massachusetts. A pixel-based error assessment was performed using the stratified sampling approach on the classified solar map. We randomly sampled 200 points within the ground-truth polygons and 200 points outside the polygons. By visually checking these 400 locations using high-resolution images from Google Earth, the overall accuracy of our solar mapping algorithm was calculated using the data from three pilot counties. For segment-based error assessment, we marked each ground truth solar polygon as detected/missed by analyzing the spatial intersections between ground truth polygons and our detected solar field polygons. The spatial quality of panels will be reported using the Jaccard index:

## _3.4.2. Validation for construction years of solar installations_

The error assessment of solar installation year at the state level was conducted based on the geocoded EIA data. Through converting the address information to a geolocation using the Google Geocoding Application Programming Interface (API) and the “ggmap” package in R, we obtained 344 location points. After checking each location based on Sentinel-2 images combined with highresolution images from Google Earth, we kept a total of 271 solar panel arrays as the validation sample. For those panels successfully detected by the COLD algorithm (267 out of 271), we compared the installation year reported by EIA and the year we detected.

## _3.5. Evaluating environmental impacts of photovoltaic power stations_

We investigated the pre-conversion land cover types by comparing the solar polygons and CDL land cover types in 2000. We calculated the area of solar arrays converted from each land cover types. To unveil the environmental impacts of solar installations, we overlaid and calculated the distances between solar installation sites with three important ecosystem function layers (i.e., wetland, pond/lake & riverine, and rare wildlife habitats).

## **4. Results**

## _4.1. Map accuracy_

The accuracy assessment suggests a relatively high overall accuracy (Fig. 6): among all the 400 sample sites, a total of 383 sites, including 141 (35.3%) Hits and 242 (60.5%) Correct Rejections, fall within the categories of correct detection, offering a successful rate of 95.8%. None of the non-solar sites were misclassified as a solar site based on our mapping approach, while missing only 4.3% of solar panel sites (n = 17). The spatial map of the detected locations shows that the missed sites are mainly located in the center of Franklin County and the northwest Hampden County.

The mean value of the Jaccard index is 0.698, suggesting a satisfactory overlap (or the degree of similarity) between the detected solar polygon and the reference polygon. Nearly half of the solar site polygons have a Jaccard index value greater than 0.8 (e.g., Fig. 7b). However, a non-trivial proportion of polygons have relatively low overlapping levels. The spatial inaccuracies are partly from that some reference polygons include tend to include cleared land surrounding the solar panels, but our mapped solar sites do not encompass the borderline space (e.g., Fig. 7c).

The accuracy assessment of construction years shows a high agreement level between COLD-detected break time and the reference construction years (Fig. 8). Among the 267 EIA-reported solar sites, 98 (36.7%) solar sites have zero bias, meaning that their identi-

## _4.2. Solar fields in Massachusetts_

A total of 703 solar arrays (2772 ha) were detected in the state of Massachusetts which could be publicly accessed from https:// taoshiqi.users.earthengine.app/view/solarpanels. Based on the distribution map (Fig. 9), all the counties have installed solar panels, and the county of Worcester has the highest number of solar arrays. The mean and median solar array area of all the solar arrays are 3.9 ha and 2.9 ha, respectively. More than half arrays (55%) have a solar array area of less than 3 ha, whereas 6% of solar arrays were built in a relatively large size (>10 ha).

The construction years of solar arrays identified by Landsat time-series analysis illustrate a low annual rate of solar installations before 2013 but an obvious spike of newly built solar arrays in recent eight years (Fig. 10), varying from less than 20 arrays per year before 2013 to a peak of 140 new arrays in 2016. After 2016, the annual number of solar installations continued to decline. The map (Fig. 10) also suggests a temporal change of spatial construction pattern: the solar arrays installed before 2015 presents no clear pattern across the state; after 2015, the newly installed arrays tend to concentrate in the central and south parts of the state, forming looming clusters.

## _4.3. Environmental changes associated with solar site construction_

By 2020, solar installations have led to conversions from multiple land cover types, among which the most prominent conversion land cover is forest, followed by cropland, grassland, and barren land. Statistically, nearly half (49%) and a quarter (23%) of the solar

sites were built upon forest and cropland, respectively. The total area of forest loss replaced by solar arrays is 1355 ha, and the total area of cropland loss replaced by the solar array is 639 ha. Specifically, the highest loss of forest converted to solar sites occurred in 2016, which is more than 600 ha of the total forest loss. Despite a decline in annual forest loss accompanying solar installations after 2016, the area of forest loss were still substantial, amounting to over 1098 ha during 2017–2019.

We evaluated the environmental impacts of solar installations through the lens of their geographic distances to ecosystems of ecological importance, including rare wildlife habitats, riverine, lakes/ponds, and wetlands (Fig. 11). The installation of photovoltaic power stations has the greatest impacts on the wildlife habitats as 426 sites (61% of the total sites) were built adjacent to rare wildlife habitats (i.e., within 500-m buffer zones), in which 38 (5%) solar sites are directly located within the habitats. There are 57 solar sites located adjacent to wetlands, 27 solar sites adjacent to the riverine and 19 solar sites located adjacent to the lake/pond.

For each county, we further calculated the median distances to all the solar stations and ranked the closest five counties (Fig. 12). In this analysis, we excluded the counties that have less than 10 sites. We found that Barnstable has the most impacted wildlife habitat by solar installations. Hampshire's solar stations are the closest to rivers. Plymouth's solar stations are the nearest to lakes, ponds and wetland comparing to other counties. Plymouth ranks the five most impacted environment in all the four analyses.

## **5. Discussion**

## _5.1. Detection of solar panel installations_

We described an efficient and accurate object-based framework for delineating solar arrays and identifying their construction years at from a combination of Sentinel-2 monthly composites and Landsat time series datasets, which is potentially generalizable for solar mapping in other regions given by that all data sources are freely accessed. The framework had a high accuracy of 95.8% success

rate for identifying the presence of solar array fields and 73.4% accuracy rate for identifying the construction time within one year. Despite some disagreements between our detection and the reference polygons, they were mainly led by the different definitions of the two data sources: some reference polygons include the surrounding cleared land while our mapping only targets on solar panel equipment area. The use of time-series dataset successfully identifies construction year at a per-site level; some earlier detections by the COLD algorithm are mainly due to that COLD was designed to detect the first spectral anomaly signal which is often attributed to land clearing/preparation, but our reference dataset targets on the completion year of solar site development.

Additionally, this analysis potentially points a way forward for mapping ground-solar installations and rooftop solar panels in urban areas. While urban areas are more spectrally and spatially heterogeneous than rural areas, there is great potential to expand the methodology explained in this study to towns and cities that are experiencing rapid growth in solar installations.

## _5.2. Solar-induced land cover change and environmental impacts_

Our mapping results show that the installation of solar panel occurs in all counties of Massachusetts. One of the most prominent solar-induced consequences is the forest loss, as 49% of solar array fields were built upon forested regions. solar-induced tree clearing may potentially result in fragmentation of large forest patches, threatening the forest ecosystem integrity and influencing the composition, structure, and function of forests (Rogan et al., 2016). Cropland is the second major land sources that solar panels were converted from (Fig. 13), which has been reported in other states such as California (Hernandez et al., 2015). Farmers used the whole or part of their land for installing solar panels, suffering a risk of decreased food production due to soil damage from construction equipment. Moreover, our GIS analysis suggests that solar field expansion affects ecosystem services particularly on wildlife habitats as more than half (61%) of the solar sites were built within 500 m of rare wildlife habitats (Fig. 11). The installation of solar panels has encroached on surrounding areas of the wildlife habitats with some even sited within the wildlife habitats, causing ecosystem fragmentation. Solar-caused deforestation, for instance, is one of the most prominent factors responsible for the reduced ecosystem services (e.g., wildlife habitat) delivered by forests (Ricci et al., 2020). The spread of solar installations also leaves unanswered questions concerning the long-term environmental impacts (Cook and McCuen, 2013; Pimentel Da Silva and Branco, 2018), including modified runoff, risk of chemical leakage from accompanying facilities, use of chemicals to maintain weed-free sites, and depletion of pollinators (Abbasi and Abbasi, 2000; Nordberg et al., 2021).

Given the rapid and widespread deployment of photovoltaic power stations in New England region and also in other places (Kruitwagen et al., 2021), timely information is needed for multiple stakeholders to understand the tradeoffs (LeMoult, 2019) between clean energy promotion and environmental conservation. Some local communities have raised concern on the damaging impacts and lowered aesthetic values to the landscape brought by the construction of solar sites (Abel, 2020). Local government agencies have been seeking solutions to achieve the optimal energy-environment balanced condition based on voices from these parties, which could be potentially addressed by our public dataset website with continued monitoring and updates.

## **6. Conclusion**

This study developed a generalizable framework to detect photovoltaic power stations by combining single-date object-based image analysis and long-term time-series analysis, and then evaluated their environmental impacts based on the satellite-based mapping results. The new photovoltaic power stations were primarily converted from forested and agricultural lands. Our result shows that solar field threatened the integrity and the functions of surrounding ecosystems such as wildlife habitats and wetlands. Our open-access photovoltaic power station dataset will be beneficial to various local stakeholders such as conservation agencies and private companies of solar energy. Relying on free satellite datasets, the mapping workflow has great potential to been applied to elsewhere in globe.
